extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof techniques / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standards for proving statements about integers, sums, recurrences and related properties using (weak and strong) mathematical induction; includes worked examples and related set-proof methods (subset, equality, power set).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of mathematical induction (Theorem 7.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fixed integer ℓ, let S = {n ∈ Z | n ⩾ ℓ}. For each integer n ∈ S, let P(n) be a statement. If P(ℓ) is true, and if the implication P(k) =⇒ P(k + 1) is true for all k ∈ S then P(n) is true for all n ∈ S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the formal condition you must satisfy to conclude a statement holds for all n ≥ ℓ. Typical proof structure: prove the basis case P(ℓ), assume P(k) (inductive hypothesis), prove P(k+1) (inductive step), then conclude by the principle. Examples in the text show starting the basis at ℓ > 1 when needed (e.g., start at n = 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard structure of an induction proof (basis + inductive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction proof consists of a Basis step — show the statement is true at the starting index — and an Inductive step — assume P(k) and prove P(k+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write proofs with a clear Basis step, state the Inductive hypothesis explicitly, perform algebra/manipulation to reach P(k+1), then conclude by induction. The text emphasizes doing 'scratchwork' to find the argument, then writing it up neatly and succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction (Corollary 7.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed ℓ, S = {n ∈ Z | n ⩾ ℓ}. If P(ℓ) is true, and if P(ℓ) ∧ P(ℓ + 1) ∧ · · · ∧ P(k) =⇒ P(k + 1) is true for all k ∈ S, then P(n) is true for all n ∈ S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong induction allows using all earlier cases up to k to prove k+1. The text shows how to derive strong induction from regular induction by defining Q(n) := 'P(ℓ),...,P(n) are all true' and applying regular induction to Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use strong induction when the inductive step requires knowledge of multiple earlier instances (not just P(k) alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated examples: existence of prime factorisation (factors a,b < k+1 require hypothesis for all n ≤ k), writing integers ≥12 as 3a+7b (prove base cases for 12,13,14 then strong step), the chocolate-bar splitting and take-away game strategies. Guidance: identify when the 'k to k+1' step needs information about earlier values and choose strong induction accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving equivalence / converting between strong and weak induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong induction and regular (weak) induction are equivalent: each can be proved from the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: from regular to strong — define Q(n) = conjunction of P(ℓ) through P(n) and apply regular induction to Q. From strong to regular — note that P(k) appears in the conjunction used by strong induction, so P(k) =⇒ P(k+1) satisfies the strong hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction with multiple base cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the inductive argument requires establishing the statement for several initial n (e.g., n = 12,13,14) before the general inductive step works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: representing integers ≥12 as sums of 3's and 7's — prove the result for several starting values (12,13,14) then use strong induction. Guidance: check whether the inductive step subtracts or adds fixed offsets that require several initial seeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics for inequality induction proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequality proofs by induction often require algebraic manipulation (e.g., multiplying the inductive hypothesis) and using the fact that k is at least the basis to strengthen bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proving 2^n ≥ n^2 for n ≥ 5 — multiply the inductive hypothesis by 2 and use k ≥ 5 to get k^2 ≥ 5k and derive k^2 ≥ 2k + 1. Text remark: 'These inequality induction problems tend to be the most tricky.' Use monotonicity and lower bounds available from k ≥ ℓ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summation identities via induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove closed forms for finite sums (e.g., sum j from a to n equals (n+a)(n+1−a)/2), use base case n=a and then assume the formula for n=k and add the (k+1)-term and simplify algebraically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard pattern: verify base, replace sum up to k with the assumed closed form, add (k+1), perform algebra to transform into closed form for k+1. The text demonstrates careful algebraic steps and bookkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction combined with calculus/analysis tools
rubrics_metrics.description: When statements involve integrals, derivatives or limits (e.g., ∫_0^∞ x^n e^{-x} dx = n!), the inductive proof may depend on calculus facts (limits, integration by parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use Fact 7.2.8 (lim_{x→∞} x^n / e^x = 0) and integration by parts to carry the inductive step; explicitly evaluate boundary terms using limits. Guidance: state and cite any calculus facts used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence / sequence identities by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove identities about recursively defined sequences (e.g., Fibonacci properties or that pn = cos(nθ) for pn defined by pn+1 = 2p1 pn − pn−1), use induction substituting recurrence relations and trigonometric identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern: establish base cases (n=0,1), assume for all ≤ k (or just k), and use the recurrence and known identities (e.g., cos addition formulas) to derive the k+1 case. Careful algebraic manipulation and substitution of recurrence terms is required; sometimes assume multiple earlier cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using helper/conjunction statements to reduce strong to weak forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Define an aggregated statement Q(n) = 'P(ℓ), P(ℓ+1), ..., P(n) are all true' to apply weak induction and thereby obtain strong conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text demonstrates this trick in proving strong induction from regular induction: Q(ℓ) holds, and Q(k)=⇒Q(k+1) follows from the strong hypothesis, so apply regular induction to Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set inclusion (A ⊆ B) and set equality
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A ⊆ B assume an arbitrary a ∈ A and show a ∈ B. To prove A = B prove both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proving 'if 6 divides a then 2 divides a' by writing a = 6ℓ and factoring. Advice: work with an arbitrary element, express it via definitions (e.g., divisibility), and conclude membership. For equality use two subset proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitivity of subset and power set inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ⊆ B and B ⊆ C then A ⊆ C. Also A ⊆ B iff P(A) ⊆ P(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove transitivity by taking arbitrary a ∈ A, deduce a ∈ B then a ∈ C. For power sets, show X ∈ P(A) ⇒ X ⊆ A and use transitivity to conclude X ⊆ B ⇒ X ∈ P(B); conversely A ∈ P(A) gives A ∈ P(B) so A ⊆ B. Use element-as-set reasoning where elements of P(A) are themselves sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-writing practice: scratchwork then succinct write-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Do exploratory scratchwork to find the structure of the argument and algebraic manipulations, then present a concise formal proof with Basis, Inductive hypothesis, Inductive step and conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frequently distinguishes between exploratory steps and the final 'Proof.' block: do messy reasoning first to identify the right manipulations/tricks, then write the polished proof. This applies across induction and set proofs.
